title: What went wrong with bluetongue — and how to prepare for the next animal disease
label: 3 November 2026 · Biosecurity and animal welfare
summary: The Committee questioned farming and veterinary leaders plus senior officials about the 2026 bluetongue outbreak. Farmers and vets described severe animal illness, reproductive losses and heavy emotional strain. Witnesses agreed the outbreak was foreseeable but communication, vaccine supply and testing delays left many exposed. Officials set out lab and reporting bottlenecks, actions underway (a vaccine strategy, lab improvements and APHA transformation) and the need for better forecasting, clearer messaging and permanent surge capacity to handle future or concurrent disease threats.

glossary.definition: A viral disease of ruminant livestock carried by midges that causes illness, deaths and fertility problems in sheep and cattle.
A recently detected virus in UK livestock with uncertain impacts and no specific treatment or vaccine yet.
Animal and Plant Health Agency: the Government agency that handles disease control and testing.
Veterinary Medicines Directorate: the agency that licences veterinary medicines and coordinates vaccine policy.
A temporary licence that lets a vaccine be used while the manufacturer collects more data for a full licence.
An organism (here, midges) that carries and transmits a disease between animals.
DEFRA-led command centre used to co-ordinate national responses to animal disease outbreaks.
APHA's transformation programme to digitise systems and create permanent surge capacity for outbreaks.

chapters.title: Multiple threats and early detection
chapters.takeaway: Bluetongue and newly detected Shamonda show the UK faces recurring, overlapping animal-disease risks that require vigilance.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We begin with bluetongue and the recent detection of Shamonda virus—another worrying threat on top of avian influenza and other outbreaks in Europe.

turns.speaker: Dr Rees
turns.text: Shamonda is new here and worrying. It was expected to arrive—surveillance picked it up in Channel Islands and Ireland—and that shows monitoring worked.

turns.speaker: Cat McLaughlin
turns.text: Farmers are concerned. Many won't have heard of Shamonda and there is no easy treatment or control, so awareness and support are needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: This highlights food security and biosecurity risks expanding beyond traditional borders, and a need for co-ordinated vigilance.

chapters.title: Impact on farms and vets
chapters.takeaway: The outbreak caused serious animal suffering, reproductive losses and severe emotional and financial pressure for farmers and heavy workloads for vets.

turns.speaker: Cat McLaughlin
turns.text: Impacts went beyond confirmed farms: deaths, severe disease, reproductive losses, lower milk and growth, extra labour and big vet bills; some losses only become clear at next lambing or calving.

turns.speaker: Dr Rees
turns.text: Clinically this season animals were sicker than before, with higher sheep mortality in the south-west. Vets could only give supportive care; there was no direct treatment.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Does the modern veterinary workforce have capacity for a localised heavy outbreak?

turns.speaker: Dr Rees
turns.text: Private vets worked hard; numbers of farm vets are lower than in 2001 and many vets have less farm experience. We need to prepare the private sector for emergency roles.

turns.speaker: Cat McLaughlin
turns.text: Farmers' margins are tight. They trust their vets, but they can't be expected to shoulder public-good costs like official testing—policy must reflect that balance.

chapters.title: Vaccination: message, cost and supply
chapters.takeaway: Vaccination is the best defence, but low early uptake, cost, misinformation and supply and pack-size issues left many vulnerable.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: Despite campaigns, why didn't earlier vaccination happen?

turns.speaker: Dr Rees
turns.text: Risk is hard to communicate. Farmers weigh uncertain benefit against cost; a new vaccine with limited early data is a tough sell. Many now wish they'd vaccinated earlier.

turns.speaker: Cat McLaughlin
turns.text: Misinformation and social media undermined confidence. The bluetongue hub (Ruminant Health & Welfare) worked well as a single information source, but farmers still struggled with cost and access.

turns.speaker: Charlie Dewhirst
turns.text: Vaccine supply ran short as Europe’s surge used stocks. How do we avoid that next year?

turns.speaker: Dr Rees
turns.text: Manufacturers can't scale instantly; stockpiles have short shelf lives. Better demand forecasting and early ordering by vets and farms are essential.

turns.speaker: Cat McLaughlin
turns.text: Pack sizes were a problem for smallholders; 50–100 dose bottles aren't suitable. We need peacetime planning on pack sizes, distribution and whether vets may split vials safely.

turns.speaker: Abigail Seager
turns.text: VMD work to authorise vaccines and to develop a five-year vaccine strategy. Supply issues showed we must improve demand forecasting and manufacturer dialogue; we brought about 5 million doses in quickly this summer.

turns.speaker: Charlie Dewhirst
turns.text: Was sharing and resale of vaccine a problem?

turns.speaker: Dr Rees
turns.text: Anecdotally yes—Facebook Marketplace and informal sharing occurred. VMD advised against resale because of cold-chain and effectiveness risks; vets ran practice broach days to help smallholders.

chapters.title: Testing, reporting and lab bottlenecks
chapters.takeaway: Late summer testing delays and reporting changes produced confusing timelines; problems included form quality, lab surge capacity and manual admin that need fixing.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: There were three-week delays in test confirmations at the peak. What impact did that have?

turns.speaker: Dr Rees
turns.text: The publicly published map was often two to three weeks out of date early on, making it harder to show localised risk and have frank conversations with farmers.

turns.speaker: Cat McLaughlin
turns.text: Some farmers waited longer than three weeks for results. That uncertainty increased emotional stress and hampered decision-making.

turns.speaker: Professor Horton
turns.text: Lab testing peaked quickly: submissions rose from ~100/week to ~150/day. Pirbright doubled and then quintupled staff efforts. Early bottlenecks were not lab capacity per se but many incomplete submission forms and the priority given to pre-movement tests.

turns.speaker: Richard Lewis
turns.text: A key bottleneck was APHA's Veterinary Exotic Notifiable Diseases Unit: small team, lots of manual checks and paperwork. They needed to validate and certify each confirmed case. The process was paper heavy.

turns.speaker: Professor Horton
turns.text: Another constraint is legal and biosecurity classification: bluetongue sits under tighter rules so labs must meet high biosafety, security and quality standards to test; designating more labs is possible but costly.

turns.speaker: Richard Lewis
turns.text: APHA is digitising reporting: a digital system will be trialled for the avian influenza season and should reduce the admin bottleneck. Bridge to Better aims to create permanent surge capacity and automate workflows.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: Devolved nations paid for testing differently. Did that affect reporting?

turns.speaker: Cat McLaughlin
turns.text: Different funding approaches across England, Wales and Scotland create inequities and mixed messages for cross-border farming; a clearer, fair approach would help surveillance.

chapters.title: Lessons, resilience and next steps
chapters.takeaway: All witnesses agree: vaccination uptake, better forecasting, lab and reporting reforms, permanent surge capacity and clearer communications are the priorities to reduce future risk.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: Can bluetongue be eradicated, or must we treat it as an ongoing seasonal risk?

turns.speaker: Professor Horton
turns.text: Theoretically controllable with a comprehensive vaccination campaign—examples in Europe show this—but practical challenges mean it may remain a recurring risk unless vaccination coverage is sustained.

turns.speaker: Richard Lewis
turns.text: The most important investment is the ability to surge at scale fast, irrespective of the specific disease. That means permanent teams, digitised systems and staff who can switch roles without burning out.

turns.speaker: Abigail Seager
turns.text: Vaccine strategy, clearer demand forecasting, and closer dialogue with manufacturers are central. Bluetongue tested emergency routes to market that we can replicate for other threats, but vaccine manufacture still takes time.

turns.speaker: Professor Horton
turns.text: Maintain national lab capability and international surveillance. Climate and vectors (midges, mosquitoes) can change risk; science and reference labs must be resourced to detect new threats like West Nile or Shamonda.

turns.speaker: Richard Lewis
turns.text: APHA's Bridge to Better includes digitisation, permanent outbreak teams and improved recruitment. Vacancy rates for vets have been reduced from ~20% to about 6% after focused recruitment efforts.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: In short: better early messaging and forecasting to get vaccine orders in early; more lab and reporting resilience; digital systems and permanent surge capacity; and clear funding choices for public-good actions.

turns.speaker: Dr Rees
turns.text: And remember the human toll: vets and farmers were under huge emotional strain. Preparedness must consider workforce wellbeing as a priority.

turns.speaker: Cat McLaughlin
turns.text: We will stay engaged. Industry and Government collaboration improved this year; that must continue so farmers understand the real risks and have practical, affordable ways to respond.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. The Committee will pursue lessons learned, funding and policy choices so the next season is handled better.
